HEADLINE: Greenback the culprit in Aussie's rise
INTRO: If there is a real villain behind the strength in the Australian dollar over the past week or so you need look no further than the United States economy. For sure, the iron ore price has had a healthy bounce, around 27 per cent since the start of the month, but it's the US dollar and the run of disappointing economic data that has been the major driver behind the local unit hitting US80¢ on Wednesday.
TEXT:
If there is a real villain behind the strength in the Australian dollar over the past week or so you need look no further than the United States economy. For sure, the iron ore price has had a healthy bounce, around 27 per cent since the start of the month, but it's the US dollar and the run of disappointing economic data that has been the major driver behind the local unit hitting US80¢ on Wednesday.

The greenback has proved to be a real menace in 2015 and not just in foreign exchange markets.

At the halfway mark of the latest US earnings season, the rise in the US dollar earlier this year, which helped send the Australian dollar to below US76¢ just a few weeks ago, has reportedly cost some of the biggest companies in America more than $US20 billion in sales.

A stronger greenback makes it more expensive for consumers in other countries to buy US goods, while a rising currency also cuts the value of revenue when US companies bring their money back home.

Buying US dollars has been a very crowded trade over the past six months or so as traders latched onto the good news coming out of the US economy and the rhetoric coming out of the Federal Reserve, which traders took to mean rising interest rates.

Most economists had thought the US economy would have grown at about 3 per cent in the first three months of this year but now it could be as low as 1.1 per cent, compared with 2.2 per cent in the last three months of 2014.

What got so many investors and traders bullish about the US dollar was the growth rate between July and September, which at 5 per cent was the fastest in more than a decade.

Investors are slated to get the latest numbers on Wednesday night, and what will be important after some disappointing data is just how bad growth is. The other issue is consumers and their state of mind. In 2014 they seemed to be happy to spend some of the money they got when the oil price fell. Households also took comfort from all the jobs that were created in the second half of 2014. But oil prices have crept higher this year and the labor market slowed noticeably in March.

The US is creating jobs, the one bright light in the economy, but not enough of the high paying ones to really help demand - and that's vital given that 70 per cent of GDP is linked to the consumer. Business investment is another indicator to watch in the report.

Making rate hikes more difficult has been some soft reports in retail sales and durable goods that reflect weakness from business and consumers.

Traders are now starting to think the rise in the currency could halt the recovery in the US before it really takes off.

That would also mean the Fed's rate rise strategy may be put on hold.

Interest rates were also at play in the local sharemarket on Wednesday. With investors going cold on the idea of a rate cut next week by the Reserve Bank of Australia, the sellers took over.

But as Andrew Fleming, deputy head of equities at Schroders, told clients this week, "Many of the traits which characterised the market boom of 2006 through 2008, before the GFC, are again in force."

Share prices have been racing ahead of earnings for a few years now and "high multiple stocks, which on the ASX are almost wholly industrial stocks with a technology and/or yield tinge, are now at multiples so high they have never before presaged gains for investors".

The other concern Fleming has is that stocks seem to be pushed around by "momentum" .

"This cannot last, as again the 2006 and 2007 markets reminded us, and the only defence from the unwinding of the momentum trade is valuation."

HEADLINE: Variables weigh on Recall bid
INTRO: On face value, the $2.7 billion takeover bid for Australia's Recall Holdings by Iron Mountain looks like a good deal. The cash and scrip offer, which Recall says is worth $8.50 per share, is well above the $5 per share the document management group was trading at last year before takeover rumours hit the market. It is also higher than the $7-per-share offer it knocked back in December.
TEXT:
On face value, the $2.7 billion takeover bid for Australia's Recall Holdings by Iron Mountain looks like a good deal. The cash and scrip offer, which Recall says is worth $8.50 per share, is well above the $5 per share the document management group was trading at last year before takeover rumours hit the market. It is also higher than the $7-per-share offer it knocked back in December.

The $US200 million ($250 million) in flagged synergies are about as high as you could expect from a takeover that had any hope of getting past regulators. There is also a clear strategic case for combining the two companies.

But the muted response to the offer from Recall shareholders reflects uncertainty around the scrip value of the offer and regulatory approvals, which are expected to take six to nine months to clear.

Recall chief Doug Pertz says there are many variables and this is exactly why shareholders should approach this offer with caution.

The actual value of Iron Mountain's offer for Recall shareholders depends on future movements in the Australian-US exchange rate between now and the end of the year when the deal is expected to close. It also depends on where the Iron Mountain share price is trading at that time.

The Recall board is assuming more upside than downside in Iron Mountain's share price. It believes there is higher value for the target's shareholders once there is a greater appreciation of the cost synergies. Iron Mountain is only forecasting US$140 million in savings, which is a reflection of the typically conservative approach boards take on the issue.

If the deal had been announced in mid-February, the scrip value would have been over $9 per share.

Pertz argues that if you take the balance of the average foreign exchange rate over the last 30 days, the deal is attractive. It also gives Recall investors a chance to share in the synergy benefits by owning a stake in Iron Mountain.

Recall's decision to back the deal rests on its confidence that there is upside in Iron Mountain's share price. Pertz says there is a higher likelihood the offer will be worth more than $8.50 a share in six to nine months' time when the bid is closed. But there are no guarantees. Deutsche Bank analysts said the offer on the table was worth $8.12, based on Iron Mountain's current share price.

If there are anti-trust issues, though, Iron Mountain should be the one wearing that risk, as the onus will be on the bidder to divest parts of the business.

Iron Mountain has offered Recall shareholders 0.1722 Iron Mountain shares for every Recall share and will provide a secondary listing on the Australian Securities Exchange.

The offer was structured with a cash alternative to protect retail investors who may not want to hold a US-listed company. This involves an option to take $8.50 per share in cash instead of the shares, although that is limited to a total cash pool of $225 million.

While the lower Australian dollar helped get the deal across the line, it was not the sole driver, and investment bankers believe exchange rates are not the main catalysts of M&A activity.

It is no longer a question of if but rather when Australia's big banks will have to introduce more stringent capital requirements.

Comments by two key players in the debate around bank capital this week suggest that changes to the way banks calculate their capital ratios will no longer wait until the rest of the world makes up its mind on the issue.

Australian Prudential Regulation Authority chairman Wayne Byres signalled a "sooner-rather-than-later" view on the issue of how much capital banks hold against mortgages while speaking at the AFR Banking & Wealth Summit on Wednesday.

His comments came a day after the chairman of the government's Financial Services Inquiry, David Murray, said it would be unwise to wait until the Basel committee completes its work on applying a floor on risk weighting used by the big four banks and Macquarie.

Byres has pointed out previously that while Australian banks are well enough capitalised to withstand an economic shock, they are not necessarily prepared to recover from a crisis.

He acknowledges we are living in a world of extremes.

Housing prices in Melbourne and Sydney have soared 42 per cent and 57 per cent respectively since 2007, according to figures published by UBS this week, which promoted its banking analyst to warn that regulators will be forced to crack down on lending practices.

Byres believes the sensible approach to tackling changes to how much capital banks have to hold against mortgages is to take it gradually but to "get started early".

"I don't think we need to be wait for every 'i' to be dotted and 't' to be crossed because the direction is clear," he says of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision process.

Byres made a similar comment in his opening statement to the House of Representatives in March when he said: "In terms of timing, we do not need to wait for every 'i' to be dotted and 't' to be crossed in the international work before we turn our minds to an appropriate response to the FSI's recommendations."

He said at the time it would also be in everyone's interests to glean a better sense of some of the likely outcomes of the international work before making too many decisions on the Australian framework.

While his stance has not shifted, Byres' "sooner rather than later" remarks on Wednesday are a first and will be interpreted as a signal the issue will be tackled this year rather than waiting for the Basel outcomes next year.

APRA's view is that once it has a better sense of the likely outcomes of the international work, it can start doing its own work locally. This will involve a extensive consultation with the industry.

Murray's comments backed a swift approach to the implementation on the inquiry's recommendations to raise the average risk weighting applied to mortgage books, something the banks oppose.

The case to move sooner rather than later is being strengthened by soaring housing prices and other threats to the Australian economy, including weaker demand for key commodity exports, such as iron ore, minerals and oil and gas. Byres says there is the potential for "fragility" and it is critical that the thinking that got financial institutions into trouble leading up to the global financial crisis should not return. While he says Australian banks have strong capital buffers, he also notes that if Basel 3 was negotiated today, it would probably have produced higher requirements.

His speech to the summit centred on the importance of balancing the need for competition with stability.

APRA now supervises far bigger and more complicated systems than in the past. The number of APRA-regulated entities was 815 with aggregated assets of $2 trillion a decade ago. At the end of last year, this was down to 600 with assets of $5 trillion.

Byres says this means the failure of an average entity is more painful and destabilising than in the past.

HEADLINE: Metcash appoints Rob Murray
INTRO: Former Lion Co and Nestle chief executive Rob Murray has been appointed chairman-elect at Metcash, strengthening the grocery wholesaler's consumer goods expertise as it attempts to reverse a two-year slide in sales and earnings.
TEXT:
Former Lion Co and Nestle chief executive Rob Murray has been appointed chairman-elect at Metcash, strengthening the grocery wholesaler's consumer goods expertise as it attempts to reverse a two-year slide in sales and earnings.

Mr Murray, who ran Nestle's Oceania business for four years and was chief executive at Lion from 2004 to 2012, transforming the beer company into Australia's biggest brewer, was appointed a non-executive director of Metcash on Wednesday and will succeed Peter Barnes as chairman after the August annual meeting.

Mr Murray was also a non-executive director of auto accessories and sporting goods retailer Super Retail Group, a major competitor of Metcash's AutoBarn business, but he stepped down on Wednesday after his appointment to the Metcash board was announced.

He remains chairman of consumer electronics retailer Dick Smith and is a non-executive director of Southern Cross Austereo, and privately owned logistics company Linfox.

Mr Barnes welcomed Mr Murray's appointment, saying he had considerable and broad-based consumer experience in fast-moving consumer goods and food and grocery retailing.

"His in-depth understanding of consumers will be a great asset to Metcash as we continue the company's transformation journey," Mr Barnes said.

Metcash is two years into a five-year turnaround plan aimed at restoring sales and earnings growth by refurbishing IGA supermarkets and reducing the gap between IGA's prices and those at Coles, Woolworths and Aldi.

The wholesaler supplies more than 2000 independent IGA retailers, who have lost market share amid mounting price competition in the $88 billion grocery market.

Metcash chief executive Ian Morrice warned in December that the wholesaler's earnings may not recover until 2017 because key elements of the turnaround plan, including a price-matching program, had taken longer than expected.

HEADLINE: Aurizon lifts iron ore haul forecasts
INTRO: Rail group Aurizon has raised its full-year iron ore haulage forecast by 2 million tonnes after starting a new contract with Perth-based miner Top Iron.
TEXT:
Rail group Aurizon has raised its full-year iron ore haulage forecast by 2 million tonnes after starting a new contract with Perth-based miner Top Iron.

Aurizon expects to haul 25 million tonnes of iron ore in fiscal 2015, up from previous guidance of 23 million tonnes despite a 17 per cent drop in haulage volumes for the quarter ending in March compared with a year earlier.

The rail operator secured a new contract in Western Australia with Top Iron, which has a strategic partnership with Chinese steel manufacturer Shanxi Jianbang, in February.

Aurizon will provide and operate wagons and locomotives to transport up to 1.5 million tonnes of iron ore annually for Top Iron's Mummaloo iron ore project east of Geraldton.

The new contract, combined with "strong railings" from existing customers, enabled Aurizon to boost its full-year guidance, the company said.

Aurizon's two biggest iron ore haulage contracts are with US group Cliffs Natural Resources and Karara Mining, controlled by China's Ansteel.

Aurizon reiterated its current annual coal haulage guidance for 210 million to 220 million tonnes after quarterly volumes rose 2 per cent compared with a year earlier to 158.6 million tonnes.

Tropical Cyclone Marcia and strikes by unions due to disputes over a new enterprise bargaining agreement hurt quarterly volumes by 2 million tonnes.

Freight volumes fell 9 per cent during the quarter, and Aurizon warned that annual freight volume growth would be "marginal", in part due to rail track damage in NSW following severe storms last week. The Hunter Valley coal rail network resumed services on Wednesday afternoon after services were suspended early last week.

Aurizon's shares, which have gained 5 per cent in the year to date, closed down 1¢ at $4.87.

Separately, engineering group Coffey International said that it would "exploit new opportunities" in transport infrastructure as the outlook improved in Australia, New Zealand and the UK.

But Coffey is pulling back from providing services to oil companies, including oil sands groups in Canada, as it restructures its business to adjust to the resources downturn.

Oil and gas services accounted for 22 per cent of Coffey's $43 million in quarterly fee revenue in its geosciences division, while mining accounted for 14 per cent.

HEADLINE: Fortescue sacks Pilbara workers
INTRO: Fortescue Metals Group has sacked about 200 people with hundreds more jobs expected to go in the coming weeks as the iron ore miner rushes to cut operating costs.
TEXT:
Fortescue Metals Group has sacked about 200 people with hundreds more jobs expected to go in the coming weeks as the iron ore miner rushes to cut operating costs.

About 100 workers at FMG's Cloudbreak mine in the Pilbara were told early on Wednesday morning to pack their bags while truck drivers who had just flown to site from Perth were told to return home immediately.

One worker told Fairfax Media the sacked drivers were taken to a recreation room, where they were told to pack up. The order to fly home surprised the workers, some of whom had been with the company for seven years.

"Nobody had any pre-warning," the source said. "They [FMG] seriously don't give a f--k about the people that have made the company successful."

The sacked workers arrived at Perth Airport just before 11am on Wednesday with plastic bags containing their belongings. Wednesday's events come after about 100 workers were flown home from FMG's Christmas Creek mine, about 30 kilometres from Cloudbreak, on Tuesday.

"They gathered the workers in a recreation room and began calling out names... some were moved to another area while those in the room were told they were going home," another source told Fairfax Media.

FMG revealed it would change its family friendly rosters on April 14, with job losses and redeployment expected.

Instead of working eight days on, six days off workers will have to work a fortnight on with one week off. The rosters will be in place across its mine sites by June 30.

A Fortescue spokesman said the roster changes were a difficult decision but was "beyond our control".

"We have communicated with our workforce consistently since the decision was announced two weeks ago," the spokesman said.

"A range of support services are available for all those impacted, including chaplaincy support, employee assistance and outplacement services."

A fixed plant operator at Christmas Creek told Fairfax Media he had almost reached Perth Airport on Tuesday when FMG rang him to say his job had been made redundant.

"They asked if [I] wanted my belongings sent home," he said.

All his tickets and licences for his machinery are among his belongings still on site.

"There's no way knowing they will pack the correct gear as we all have shared accommodation," he said.

The operator said he had emailed FMG about his redundancy package and retrieval of personal belongings but had not heard a reply.

"[There's] not much loyalty, they could've at least flown me up so I could've packed my own stuff," he said.

Most of the workers who flew to Christmas Creek yesterday were sent home immediately.

"About 90 per cent of the operators at the fixed plant at Christmas Creek got made redundant, so there doesn't seem to be more redeployment going on," he said..

Analysts estimated Fortescue could shed more than 700 jobs due to the roster changes.

The new rosters do not require as many workers to extract the same rate of production.

Earlier this month, AWU Western Australia branch secretary Stephen Price estimated about 10 per cent of the workforce were likely to lose their jobs.

Fortescue employs about 4800 people, with more than 4000 working across its Pilbara operations. Thousands of contractors also work at its mines.

"I think it's very underhanded what Fortescue is doing," Mr Price said.

HEADLINE: Nufarm sues over weed data leak
INTRO: Crop protection manufacturer Nufarm is suing the federal government for negligence after confidential information about two of its weed killer products was handed to its competitors.
TEXT:
Crop protection manufacturer Nufarm is suing the federal government for negligence after confidential information about two of its weed killer products was handed to its competitors.

Nufarm claims it lost sales and profit margin to its key competitors - Malaysian crop protection heavyweight Kenso and local outfits 4Farmers Australia and Conquest Crops - after its secret formulas and proprietary mixing instructions were passed on to its rivals through a product approval process.

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) handles that process and is defending the case Nufarm has launched in the Supreme Court of Victoria seeking unspecified damages, compensation, interest and costs.

The company has declined to quantify to Fairfax Media the damages it's seeking for its loss of sales in the local herbicide market that brought in revenues of more than $400 million in full-year 2014.

In recent years, Nufarm has seen the contribution from the sale of herbicide products in its Australian business wither from $417 million in 2013 to $411.9 million in 2014. For the first half of 2015 the company booked $157 million in revenues from its Australian herbicide business.

APVMA chief executive Kareena Arthy declined to comment.

At no point does Nufarm allege any misconduct or inappropriate behaviour by its competitors. Representatives from Kenso and Conquest declined to comment.

Nufarm alleges it spent millions developing new crop products that were able to remove a particularly stubborn and herbicide-resistant rye grass from Australian farms.

According to the company, the new product involved a complex mixing process and application process of two existing herbicides - triallate and trifluralin.

Nufarm claims that the information it provided to APVMA to obtain a permit for the use and labelling of its new herbicide product was secret at the time.

4Farmers general manager Neil Mortimore said he was perplexed by Nufarm's application, saying that the concept of mixing the two chemicals was "as old as the hills".

"I'd be really concerned if this case was successful as it could have major ramifications.

"Watch out Australian farmers your prices for chemicals are about to go up," Mr Mortimore said.

In 2009, Kenso was granted permission by the authority to replicate Nufarm's mixing instructions on their own product labels, according to Nufarm.

Nufarm alleges it raised questions over Kenso's permit at the time and was assured the APMVA database would be updated to ensure its proprietary information was not passed on to its competitors.

However, the authority allegedly failed to inform Nufarm that it had earlier in 2009 approved 4Farmers's product and labelling, which also relied on Nufarm's formulas.

Conquest later allegedly relied on 4Farmers' permit in its own application for a permit for a similar product.

"The APVMA owed a duty to Nufarm to take reasonable care to protect the protected information and the Nufarm mixing instructions from being exploited by Nufarm's competitors," the company said in its statement of claim.

Nufarm also alleges APVMA committed misfeasance in public office claiming it passed on the information with "reckless indifference" and caused the company losses.

Key points

Nufarm says secret formulas and proprietary mixing instructions were passed on to its rivals.

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority is defending the case, filed in Victoria.

HEADLINE: Aussie surges on greenback weakness
INTRO: The dollar rose above US80¢ overnight Tuesday after weak economic data in the United States, iron ore's price rally and a reduced chance of rate cuts from the Reserve Bank of Australia conspired to lift the currency to the highest level since January.
TEXT:
The dollar rose above US80¢ overnight Tuesday after weak economic data in the United States, iron ore's price rally and a reduced chance of rate cuts from the Reserve Bank of Australia conspired to lift the currency to the highest level since January.

By 4.20pm AEST on Wednesday, the Aussie had settled back to US79.93¢.

Before the first-quarter US economic growth figure due on Wednesday and a meeting of the Federal Reserve this week, consumer confidence in the world's largest economy declined in April, adding support to a view that the Fed will have to wait longer before raising rates.

That suggests September is now the earliest window for the first hike since the financial crisis, which dragged the US dollar down and sent US 10-year Treasury yields higher to 1.98 per cent.

The dollar was selling for US79.93¢ late on Wednesday and at one point was up about 2 per cent to US80.26¢. Iron ore rose 1.3 per cent overnight Tuesday to $US59.88 a tonne.

A recovery in the price of iron ore amid a broad rally in commodities has returned the Australian currency to favour.

The upswing in commodity prices could also mean the RBA is less convinced of the need to stimulate the economy with a rate cut when it meets next week following a modest improvement in domestic economic data.

Market pricing on the probability of a one-quarter of a percentage point reduction in rates to 2 per cent next Tuesday has slipped to a 45 per cent chance.

"We've seen an improvement in the iron ore price off the lows, which has taken away fears we were heading to $US35 [a tonne]," said ANZ's senior currency strategist, Daniel Been.

"At the same time, we've seen a little bit of position clearing ahead of the FOMC. What's interesting is Aussie and Kiwi have been outperformers."

Mr Been did not anticipate sentiment towards the Australian dollar turning positive but for the time being, absent any volatility in the market, the carry trade had "come back into vogue".

"You'll always have these periods when volatility dips ... I certainly don't think this is the beginning of an extended rally in the Aussie dollar."

Economists were almost unanimous in forecasting a cut at the May meeting a few weeks ago but better employment data for March and slightly improved inflation for the first quarter have dented the urgency of any RBA action. A majority of economists still have a May cut in their sights.

The appreciation of the Australian dollar will be met with great frustration by the central bank; indeed all of the currency benefit of the February rate cut has now been wiped out.

The Australian dollar is overvalued in the RBA's eyes and in the minutes of the April meeting, the RBA predicted that "further depreciation of the Australian dollar was likely given the recent declines in key commodity prices".

Commonwealth Bank of Australia chief currency and rates strategist Richard Grace said strong Australian dollar interest could endure for the next six weeks or so if the Fed delivered a doveish statement and the RBA signalled an unwillingness to cut further.

"It is an important week and that will be a big factor in determining whether the Australian dollar can carry on with this lift," he said.

"I suspect that the Australian dollar can carry on because it's not just driven by the US dollar but supply-driven cuts in commodity prices. The lift we've had in iron ore and oil prices and some of the other commodities as well is helpful."

Mr Grace said that broadly he expected the Australian dollar to be weaker but it could add a few cents if conditions were supportive. It is 6 per cent higher now than its 2015 low.

Another factor at play helping the Australian currency was that European Central Bank stimulus is keeping a lid on the value of the euro, which also rose against the greenback overnight Tuesday, but is not responding as sharply to better euro area economic signals because of the ECB's commitment to quantitative easing.

The euro gained 0.8 per cent to $US1.0973 after achieving the highest value since April 6.

The euro also capitalised on optimism that Greece was making progress on talks with the eurogroup over its credit lifeline.

HEADLINE: Banks lead market to worst day of the year
INTRO: The Australian sharemarket suffered its biggest fall of the year, led down by the big banks amid growing doubts the Reserve Bank of Australia will cut interest rates next week, as a surge in the Australian dollar worried investors.
TEXT:
The Australian sharemarket suffered its biggest fall of the year, led down by the big banks amid growing doubts the Reserve Bank of Australia will cut interest rates next week, as a surge in the Australian dollar worried investors.

The S&P/ASX 200 closed down 109.94 points, or 1.85 per cent, to 5838.6, while the broader All Ordinaries fell 103.25 points to 5818.2.

The Australian dollar hit a three-month high of US80.25¢ overnight, as the greenback weakened and investors speculated the recent run of stronger-than-expected local economic data and the iron ore price rally could stay the RBA board's hand next Tuesday.

The day's falls were led by rates-sensitive banks, with Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Westpac Banking Corp, National Australia Bank and ANZ Banking Group all losing around 2 per cent. CBA fell 2.2 per cent to $90.57, Westpac lost 2.6 per cent to close at $37.40, while NAB fell 2.4 per cent to $37.46 and ANZ lost 1.9 per cent to close at $34.75.

The jump in the Australian dollar also hit companies that report in US dollars, including Sims Metal Management which lost 6.8 per cent to $10.77, Ansell fell 4.9 per cent to $26.10, James Hardie lost 4.7 per cent to close at $14.40 and CSL was hit 4.4 per cent to finish at $91.

A Goldman Sachs report that Australia is at risk of losing its coveted AAA credit rating may have sparked some additional fear among investors.

The US investment bank cited a likely further deterioration in public finances as a key reason for Standard & Poor's to consider a change in the rating. A cut was also likely to lead to downgrades of the big banks, which currently hold an AA- rating, Goldman added.

The day's fall could also be attributed to nervousness ahead of the US Federal Open Market Committee rates decision on Thursday morning Australian time, Patersons economic strategist Tony Farnham said.

"It's becoming even more intense, the will-they-or-won't-they effect with regards to judgement," he said.

Signs that the recent iron ore price rally may be fading, with Chinese iron ore futures down 3 per cent, hit Fortescue Metals Group, which fell 7.4 per cent to $2.27. BHP Billiton lost 1.2 per cent closing at $32.04, while Rio Tinto fell 1.8 per cent to $57.71.

Morgans private client adviser Alistair McCorquodale downplayed the two-day losses, saying the broader context of gains and closing in on the 6000 mark was more significant.

"I think people were more comfortable as the dollar was weakening against the US dollar because it was increasing our competitiveness, as investors you start to become more comfortable that you're able to compete effectively," he said.

"When you're a commodity-based export country and you have declining US dollar exports, that weakening provides a cushion."

But a strong run in the first quarter of 2015 has investors questioning whether equities have run too hard and are overpriced, Dalton Nicol Reid director Jamie Nicol said.

"Certainly the PE [price-earnings] of the market at 16.3-times is looking high by recent historic standards.

"However the dilemma for the market is that it has rarely looked cheaper relative to the current low bond yields and interest rates," he said.

"Given the size of the market's move [11 per cent year to date], a pullback is quite possible."

Other movers of the day included IAG, which closed down 4.1 per cent lower to $5.65 after lowering its full-year insurance margin guidance in the wake of the Sydney storms last week.

Upbeat sales data from Wesfarmers failed to buoy the company's shares, dipping slightly 0.4 per cent to $43.

The big winners of the day were energy stocks including MMA Offshore, which added 5.4 per cent, Northern Star which added 3.6 per cent per cent, and AWE which gained 3 per cent.

HEADLINE: Kmart's gain is Target's pain
INTRO: Discounter Kmart is cannibalising sales at sister chain Target, highlighting the dilemma for Wesfarmers as it attempts to reverse a five-year slide in earnings at the department store chain and justify its continued presence in the conglomerate's portfolio.
TEXT:
Discounter Kmart is cannibalising sales at sister chain Target, highlighting the dilemma for Wesfarmers as it attempts to reverse a five-year slide in earnings at the department store chain and justify its continued presence in the conglomerate's portfolio.

Wesfarmers has blamed a steeper than expected 3.2 per cent slide in same-store sales at Target in the March quarter on gains at Kmart, where same-store sales rose 5.5 per cent, adjusted for Easter, the fastest pace for five years.

Kmart opened two new stores and refurbished eight, lifting total sales by almost 11 per cent to $937 million, taking share from Target and Woolworths' BIG W chain, which is expected to reveal negative sales growth when it reports next week.

"We have certainly seen some cannibalisation and some categories that Kmart did well in Target had difficult times, so there's a bit of cannibalisation," Wesfarmers finance director Terry Bowen said on Wednesday. However, chief executive Richard Goyder reaffirmed his commitment to retaining two discount department stores in the Wesfarmers stable, saying Target was showing positive signs in key measures such as customer transactions, unit growth and the proportion of full-price sales, and in key categories such as childrenswear.

"We are on a similar journey at Target as we were at Kmart," Mr Goyder said. "We had (adviser and UK retail expert) Archie Norman out last week and he says we're reaching some of the milestones at Target that we reached early on at Kmart."

When Wesfarmers acquired the Coles Group for $20 billion in 2007, Kmart was the worst performer in the group and was facing an uncertain future. Now Kmart is one of the best performers after lifting sales by 5 per cent and earnings by 86 per cent over the last five years.

Kmart's gains have come at the expense of Target, where sales have fallen more than 8 per cent and earnings have tumbled 77 per cent in five years, reducing its return on capital to just 2.9 per cent last year.

Mr Goyder believes both businesses are capable of growing simultaneously by gaining customer trust in prices and keeping their offers relevant.

"We've always kept the businesses separate and made sure we don't tie the hand of each divisional managing director behind their back," he said. "We've been providing capital to (Kmart MD Guy Russo) to grow that business and you can see the results, at same time we've supported (Target MD Stuart Machin) with capital where he needs it."

"We understand from time to time those businesses compete with each other (and) frankly we don't mind that - it's not as if it's a two-player market.

HEADLINE: Tatts CEO splashes cash for rebrand
INTRO: Tatts Group chief executive Robbie Cooke has a new wagering brand and he's not afraid to use it.
TEXT:
Tatts Group chief executive Robbie Cooke has a new wagering brand and he's not afraid to use it.

Mr Cooke on Wednesday revealed a raft of new sporting sponsorships that will form part of a multimillion-dollar marketing spend to promote the new UBET wagering brand and challenge market leader Tabcorp, as well as fast-growing online-only rivals like William Hill Australia and Sportsbet.

Tatts, alongside Tabcorp, is one of the incumbent retail wagering operators and has exclusive licences to operate bricks-and-mortar wagering outlets in Queensland, South Australia, Northern Territory and Tasmania. But the $6 billion company's wagering arm Tattsbet has lagged the competition as Tatts focused on its highly profitable lotteries arm.

In the $13 billion online wagering market, Tatts has fallen behind Tabcorp and its new British-backed rivals William Hill and Sportsbet to be fourth by market share. Now, two years after the Brisbane-based company first began working with a design agency on a rebrand, Mr Cooke is making up for lost time. "Tatts in the past has not engaged in wagering marketing activity to any major extent," he said. "This is the first time that we're out there actually fighting back. In Australia we are the largest non-casino gambling group. It is time to start behaving as the market leader."

In addition to its existing sponsorships of some racing carnivals and AFL team the Gold Coast Suns, UBET will sponsor the Port Adelaide Football Club, V8 Supercars and Melbourne City Football Club. The company has also rounded up prominent athletes to act as ambassadors and provide commentary on its betting website, including AFL player Jonathan Brown, the NRL's Anthony Minichiello, and former Wallabies rugby union captain Nathan Sharpe.

Mr Cooke said a recent deal that Tatts had struck with Queensland Racing, which cut some of the fees it had to pay the group, freed up $15 million that it could spend on marketing without "any detriment to the bottom line". "We can spend that or we can go higher," he said. "We will act in our commercial interest as we push out."

The new brand name and its black-and-green livery will be rolled out to Tatts' 1200 retail outlets over three to five years. Mr Cooke dismissed the idea that such a huge marketing push was a waste of money, given many of the outlets will be operating without the new branding at first. "If we see a stronger sales outcome than we are anticipating, it will give us the ability to speed up that roll-out," Mr Cooke said.

Alongside the rebrand, Tatts has unveiled a suite of improved digital betting offerings, including a new website and smartphone app. Bets placed online make up 25 per cent of Tatts' wagering revenue.

In response to a report in The Australian on Wednesday saying Tabcorp was weighing a takeover of Tatts' wagering arm, Mr Cooke said he had "not had any conversations with anybody about our wagering asset".
